cues.text: Hallo und willkommen zurück bei German for Beginners – Deutsch für Anfänger!
In the last German lesson we learned how to ask for someone's age, occuptation and origin
in German, and of course respond to these questions as well.
In today's learning German lesson you will learn how to count up to a trillion in German
and how to say 1st, 2nd and so on!
Let's start – Lasst uns anfangen!
We'll begin by learning how to count from 0-20 in German:
Null (0), eins (1), zwei (2), drei (3), vier (4), fünf (5), sechs (6), sieben (7), acht
(8), neun (9), zehn (10) Instead of saying zwei, some people say "zwo"
to avoid confusion with "drei".
For example when reading out a telephone number.
Let's now learn how to count from 11-20 in German!
Elf (11), zwölf (12), dreizehn (13), vierzehn (14,), fünfzehn (15), sechzehn (16), siebzehn
(17), achtzehn (18), neunzehn (19), zwanzig (20)
To say the 1st, 2nd and so on you say: der erste, der zweite, der dritte, der vierte,
der fünfte, der sechste, der siebte, der achte, der neunte, der zehnte.
Can you see the pattern here?
Mostly you just add "te" to the end to say 1st, 2nd and so on!
But once it reaches 20 you add "ste" - 22nd "der zweiundzwanzigste", 35th "der fünfunddreißigste",
"ste".
And so on, and so on, and so on!
Let's now count from 20 to 30! einundzwanzig, zweiundzwanzig, dreiundzwanzig,
vierundzwanzig, fünfundzwanzig, sechsundzwanzig, siebenundzwanzig, achtundzwanzig, neunundzwanzig,
dreißig.
Can you see the pattern?
We use the numbers from 1-9, add an "und" and the main number which in this case is
20. Zwanzig.
This is the same for all the main German numbers up to 100.
31 = einunddreißig, 42 = zweiundvierzig, 53 = dreiundfünfzig, 64 = vierundsechzig,
75 = fünfundsiebzig, 86 = sechsundachtzig, 97 = siebenundneunzig and 100 = (ein)hundert
From 100 onwards, things change a bit: 101 is (ein)hunderteins, 102 is (ein)hundertzwei,
103 is (ein)hundertdrei and so on.
For 110 you say "(ein)hundertzehn", 111 is "(ein)hundertelft.
It's optional to say einhundert or simply hundert when it comes to the number 100.
Once you've reached 1000 the pattern repeats itself – 1000 = (ein)taunsend, 1001 = (ein)tausendeins,
1224 = (ein)tausendzweihundertvierundzwanzig and so on.
2000 is zweitausend.
The rest of the thousands continue in the same way up to...
9999 = neuntausendneunhundertneunundneunzig Let's now take a look at the big numbers up
to a trillion. 10.000 = zehntausend, 20.000 = zwanzigtausend
, 100.000 = (ein)hunderttausend , 1.000.000 = (eine) Million, 2.000.000 = zwei Millionen
In German we say "eine Million" for one million while two million is "zwei Millionen".
Take note that we use a decimal point instead of a comma!
A billion is "eine Milliarde".
While an English billion is a German Milliarde, a German Billion is an English trillion.
So a trillion is "eine Billion" in German.
So, there you have it!
Now you now how to count in German!
Good job!
Gute Arbeit!
